entries.title: Troops ‘Can’t Feel Genuinely Safe’ as Trump Weighs Iran Escalation
entries.summary: Current and former military officials warn that fear of retaliation by Iran and the prospect of increased deployment length is adding to service members’ wariness.
entries.content:
As President Donald Trump considers resuming attacks on Iran, there are growing fears among U.S. troops in the Middle East and veterans of past wars in the region that escalation would invite retaliation and prolong a monthslong conflict.

“Service members continue to exist in a vulnerable state where at any moment things could happen again … they can’t feel genuinely safe,” said a U.S. official familiar with conditions among active-duty troops stationed at U.S. bases in Persian Gulf countries. “Throughout the war, we have had these sophisticated systems [for defense] but they aren’t perfect.”

Tehran dealt significant damage to American bases in countries like Kuwait and Bahrain earlier in the year, shattering what the official and other sources described as a perception in the military that deployments there were relatively secure. According to the Pentagon, at least 23 service members have been killed and 865 wounded since Trump launched the war in February. Administration critics say this is probably an undercount, as the Pentagon has withheld casualty numbers and acknowledgement of some Iranian strikes, citing operational security. Democratic lawmakers have demanded answers from the Pentagon about discrepancies in its count. Around 50,000 U.S. troops are positioned in the Middle East following Trump’s orders for the biggest buildup in the area since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Though officials and reports suggest the Trump administration has recently moved personnel away from some bases ahead of a possible escalation, members of the military community told The Washington Sun that informal discussions about the war highlight peril and exhaustion, with some U.S. troops still at facilities that have been partially destroyed.

A reservist previously deployed to the Middle East said that in their network, which includes active-duty colleagues, there is significant opposition to a new back-and-forth with Iran and doubts about military leadership.

“Many of them feel like they are in a religious war against Muslims,” said the reservist, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has suggested God backs the U.S. in the Iran war, emphasized historic conflict between Christians and Muslims and cast Muslim immigration as a threat.

Additionally, the reservist said “everyone is concerned” about Hegseth’s firing of a respected top military planner, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, whom the Pentagon accused of leaking classified information. Those claims have not been independently verified.

The U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, told The Sun troops have been strained by multiple extensions to their deployments, in some cases being notified the day before they were supposed to leave. And some have been told they are deployed indefinitely after initially being told they would be sent to the region for a few weeks on a so-called “deterrence deployment.”

Troop frustration goes well beyond deployment length, the official said, noting that some of the greatest concern has been about what’s happened when bases come under assault. Orders to shelter in bunkers often came with too little time for troops to reach the bunkers. Even in the bunkers, generally designed to shield from shrapnel rather than direct strikes, service members were vulnerable to concussions. And some bunkers lacked doors, so personnel watched the live destruction of their facilities. Some troops were directed to leave their bases, the official said, and head into the surrounding desert.

Among those who have been evacuated from the region, many are receiving medical retirements, separations or limitations on future work, the official added, casting doubt on CENTCOM statements that 95% quickly returned to duty.

“I have seen folks who were probably kept in-theater longer than they should have been … their condition was deteriorating and expected to continue to do so. They weren’t really combat-effective,” the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, defended Trump’s war strategy and said he appreciates U.S. troops.

“President Trump has been consistent even before holding public office: Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. The President took decisive action to eliminate this threat and, thanks to his bold leadership, the American people are already safer. Our brave men and women in uniform have embodied American strength and resilience, and their Commander in Chief is grateful for their honorable service,” Wales said in a statement to The Sun.

A spokesperson for Hegseth directed queries to CENTCOM, the U.S. military command overseeing Middle East operations. Representatives for CENTCOM did not respond to requests for comment.

Sam Scanlon, a former Army officer who is now senior vice president of the Truman National Security Project, noted the perception of the Iran war is different from that of past U.S. offensives, such as the targeting of the Islamic State, which benefited from broader public backing.

“For this war with very little support, that takes a mental toll not only on the service member but on the family, too,” said Scanlon, who told The Sun he has repeatedly heard from his former colleagues in the region that their bases are “hammered” without sufficient deflection resources.

Some veterans of America’s post-9/11 War on Terror campaigns supported Trump because he “campaigned as a peace president” and created the expectation the U.S. would “regroup,” Scanlon added.

Trump’s war, current and former military personnel and other national security observers fear, has no clear exit strategy — leaving U.S. forces stretched thin amid other international concerns.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) said Thursday he had seen an Iran war plan that “is insane … and will set off a new cycle of escalation.” Earlier in the week, Gen. Ronald Clark, the top Army officer in the Pacific, publicly predicted Beijing will be militarily prepared next year to capture the self-governing island of Taiwan.

The depletion of American weapons, redirecting forces away from the South China Sea and skepticism among U.S. allies about decision-making in Washington could all undercut any U.S. response to Beijing, Scanlon said.

Iran’s ability to retaliate despite U.S. sanctions pressure and a troop buildup, the official said, is “exposing American vulnerability more broadly.”

Meanwhile, they added, “we’re asking a lot of service members right now, and what we’re asking of them may not be sustainable forever.”

In an email to The Sun, a White House official said the U.S. military “has more than enough resources to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and counter any foreign threats.”

The Trump administration is seeking $67 billion in additional military funding to resupply munitions used during the Iran war.

Trump’s team has recently suggested it sees a possibility for diplomacy with Iran’s new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei. But experts say Iran remains unlikely to make the sweeping concessions sought by Trump.

Kris Goldsmith, a combat veteran and the president of a group of military-linked content creators called the Valor Media Network, told The Sun that the frustration extends beyond service members.

He pointed to the family of Nicholas McKelvey, who jumped off the U.S.S. Lincoln, the aircraft carrier that was deployed for a record-breaking uninterrupted time at sea, after missing the birth of his daughter and expressing concerns about his mental health to his wife.

“We hope Congress is paying attention,” said Goldsmith, adding that he anticipated future Capitol Hill hearings about “the carelessness with which our troops and their families are being treated.”
entries.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed

entries.title: FBI Blames North Korea for Stolen Billions From Binance in Biggest Hack in History
entries.summary: The FBI said the attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor.
entries.content:
By Bernard Condon

The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.

The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.”

Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved.

“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.

Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

“It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.”

He added: “It’s just this cat and mouse game.”

On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.

The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.

Associated Press writer Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Inside the Effort to Get Americans in Canada to Vote
entries.summary: Some Canadians, angry about Trump’s tariff war and other cross-border policies, are working to get many of the more than 600,000 Americans who live in Canada to vote in the midterms.
entries.content:
Miraculously, no one got a paper cut. But at least one volunteer mailing American get-out-the-vote flyers from a Toronto public library would have been fine with a little bloodshed.

“It’s for democracy,” Maya Stevens-Uninsky said, stamping “Election Materials” onto yet another envelope.

Stevens-Uninsky is one of more than 40 Toronto residents who volunteered at a “Democracy Action Hub” run out of the Deer Park neighborhood library by the local chapter of Democrats Abroad. In addition to sending 1,800 postcards, the volunteers texted 400 members registered to vote in Michigan, passed out yard signs reading “Americans can vote! from Canada,” stapled posters to telephone poles and set up “Vote From Abroad” tables at every street fair and neighborhood corn roast they could.

Their goal: Persuade Americans living in Canada to vote in the U.S. midterms during an election cycle in which the Republican Party and the Trump administration have imposed a series of challenges on overseas voters. The administration has removed guidance on overseas voting from a federal website; tried to give the U.S. Postal Service unprecedented oversight of voting by mail; and sued eight of the 38 states that allow Americans raised overseas to cast ballots in a parent’s home state, winning that challenge in North Carolina.

“There’s a lot of desire to participate when you feel that your right to vote is being threatened,” said Valencia Richardson, a senior legal counsel at the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center. “There is real energy from Americans abroad to participate in the midterms.”
Democrats Abroad Get Out the Vote Action Hub (7625x5083, AR: 1.50)Democrats Abroad Get Out the Vote Action Hub (5088x3392, AR: 1.50)The largest population of Americans abroad lives in Canada: 612,780 people, according to the latest U.S. government estimates from 2024. That means 1.5% of Canada’s population are Americans with permanent resident status, naturalized dual citizens and dual citizens born abroad. (The United Kingdom is a distant second, with 327,528 Americans, followed by Mexico with 313,602.) Add President Donald Trump’s tariff war, his attempt to rename Lake Ontario and a slew of other policies making cross-border relations more challenging — such as falsely accusing Canada of being a major source of illegal fentanyl imports — and you have a swath of angry Canadians urging eligible Americans to vote.

Julie Buchanan, a soft-spoken Alabamian who is chair of Democrats Abroad Toronto, declined to share how many members her chapter has, “but it’s in the thousands,” she said. In the weeks leading to the election, she has fielded about 10 requests a day from Toronto-area Americans who want help voting. She even drove to one older voter’s home and sat beside the woman as she registered to vote in the States and requested a ballot for the first time.

“That took hours,” Buchanan said. Like many Democrats Abroad volunteers, Buchanan moved north after marrying a Canadian; she met a man from Ontario at a blues festival in Mississippi. Austin Pettigrew, another volunteer for the organization, has a similar story: He joined an online dating app in Rochester, New York, and set the mileage radius wide enough to date in Syracuse. The algorithm matched him with a Canadian across the lake instead.

“We’d been chatting for a while before we realized we were in different countries,” Pettigrew recalled. He and his now-wife bonded over similar values and trips to do humanitarian work in developing countries. Volunteering at a Democracy Action Hub and posting a midterms sign in his Toronto yard was a natural extension of that activism, he said.

Jobs and educational opportunities, not dating apps, are the more traditional ways Americans end up in Canada.

University of Toronto sophomore Emily Chen said she plans to vote for Democrat James Talarico in Texas’ toss-up Senate race. She learned about the university’s Vote From Abroad club on Instagram and joined an energized group of students writing postcards at the library.

“I’m thinking about writing, ‘Vote now so you can later,’” Chen said, holding a pen and looking at her friends for guidance. “Is that too morbid?”

Nearly all Americans abroad have been guaranteed the right to vote in federal elections since 1972. The 2009 federal MOVE Act brought overseas voting into the internet age and required states to mail ballots at least 45 days before the election. The legislation also recommended — but did not require — that states extend voting rights to Americans born abroad who have not lived in the United States. Beyond those guidelines, however, states have considerable control over overseas voting.

Chen grew up in Plano, near Dallas, and found voting as a Texan in Canada in 2025 to be cumbersome at best. “You can’t do anything online other than check if you’re registered,” she said.

The first week of November happens to be a study break at the university, so she opted to fly home this year.

Americans crossing borders to cast ballots is one reason Amanda Klekowski von Koppenfels, an international elections scholar at the University of Kent, believes the official U.S. government figure of 247,295 Americans voting from overseas in the 2024 general election — out of an estimated 2.2 million people who were eligible — is too low. Anyone who voted in person didn’t make that head count.

“A lot of people do it,” Klekowski von Koppenfels said. “We just don’t know how many.”
Democrats Abroad Get Out the Vote Action Hub (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Dems in Canada Voting (7306x4870, AR: 1.50)She suspects bridge-and-tunnel voting is particularly prevalent in Windsor, Ontario, where an estimated 20% of the city’s population — about 41,000 people — are Americans, some of whom commute to Michigan for work.

“We have a very intensive effort there,” said Democrats Abroad international chair Martha McDevitt-Pugh. In 2024, Michigan tallied 21,128 overseas ballots; Democrat Elissa Slotkin won her U.S. Senate seat by 19,006 votes.

“Pretty much everybody in Windsor knows an American, if they’re not an American themselves,” McDevitt-Pugh said.

Swing-state status helped motivate Toronto resident Josh Hall to vote in the midterms. Hall moved from Charlotte to Toronto in 2022 after he was invited to join the National Ballet of Canada. He voted by mail in 2024 but became concerned this year that a Trump administration rule turning over their voter rolls to the U.S. Postal Service — a move ultimately shot down by the Supreme Court in mid-September — could disenfranchise overseas voters.

“I was worried about my vote not counting,” he said.

Fortunately for Hall, North Carolina is one of two dozen states that allows Americans voting from overseas to use an electronic portal, even though it’s a multistep process and, as Hall lamented, “I didn’t get a sticker” like he did in 2024. During both election cycles, he and another American in the ballet company struck up an accountability partnership to keep track of deadlines and where their ballots were in the pipeline.

“We knew we needed to be on top of it,” he said.

Hall voted for Democrat Roy Cooper in North Carolina’s tight Senate race, and in conversations with Americans in the States, he’s tried to explain, as diplomatically as he can, how Trump’s policies have affected Canadians.

“That’s why I’m voting,” Hall said. “I’m voting because I care about my friends and family back home, and I care about the country where I’m living now.”
entries.author: Rebecca Ritzel

entries.title: Judge Dismisses a Trump-Backed Lawsuit in the Alaska Ballot Case
entries.summary: The Trump administration was seeking to block certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race if GOP incumbent loses.
entries.content:
JUNEAU, Alaska — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.

Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in one of the country’s most closely watched races, with Senate control at stake. Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name.

The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and with early voting underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.

U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the United States seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots. She said the cast ballots been commingled to the point where the identity of the person who cast each ballot can’t be determined.

“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified “investigation” of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.

This is a developing story and has been updated with further information.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Sen. Chris Murphy Hospitalized After a Stroke
entries.summary: He is "awake and alert" and expected to make a full recovery, his office said.
entries.content:
Sen. Chris Murphy “experienced a stroke” on Saturday, the Connecticut Democrat’s office said in a statement.

“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” his office said Sunday morning.

Murphy is receiving treatment at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland, his office said.

Murphy is one of the more high-profile Senate Democrats and is a member of party leadership in the chamber. He’s also considered a potential presidential candidate for 2028.
entries.author: Igor Bobic

entries.title: Haley Stevens Breaks With Her Party to Back Republican Mike Rogers
entries.summary: Stevens started a feud with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, culminating in an appearance that signaled support of his opponent.
entries.content:
DETROIT, Michigan — Rep. Haley Stevens on Sunday endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race, accelerating the string of headaches she’s caused for Democrats in the eleventh hour of a critical race in Michigan between Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

“I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today. I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, going on to say that she’s still “a very proud Democrat.”

Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday. In a clip shared by a local reporter, Stevens said she’s for investing in Black-owned businesses and “that is a policy that Mike’s going to take on.”

Rogers’ campaign referred The Washington Sun to her endorsement post.

A spokesperson for Stevens responded to an inquiry by referring The Sun to a tweet reporting the news that Stevens’ official staff were resigning from her office on Sunday.

Stevens was originally slated to appear with El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) at another church for a Souls to the Polls event on Sunday, but she was ultimately uninvited after needling El-Sayed over his criticism of Israel, creating a distracting intraparty feud in the final stretch of the close contest.

El-Sayed’s campaign previously told The Sun that they had asked Stevens not to attend campaign events in the final days before the election after Friday’s dust-up. Later on Saturday, Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Michigan) told CNN that she had rescinded the invitation because “there’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place for the next few days.”

On Friday, Stevens rebuked El-Sayed for his criticism of Israel and demanded that he apologize for his past comments. Her fiance, Jason Turkish, said last week that he planned to vote for Rogers.

‘"It is still unclear to me how he went from donor to fiancé," a source familiar with the inner workings of Stevens’ Senate campaign told The Sun. "I have not talked to either of them since August, but I think it's the two of them against the world now."

It’s unclear that any of this will ultimately affect voter sentiment, but it’s a distraction in an election that had otherwise pulled together most factions of the Democratic Party.

“The people that were all pro-Israel and stuff, they weren't going to vote for him anyhow. So I'm not sure if it made that big of a difference, but it sure showed her colors,” said Jackie, an El-Sayed supporter who declined to give her last name, at a get-out-the-vote rally on Saturday.

Her appearance immediately drew criticism from national and state Democrats.

“Standing with Miker Rogers is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career. It's also a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, on social media.

—
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Calls Haley Stevens a ‘Distraction’
entries.summary: “At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens,” he said at an event she was originally scheduled to participate in.
entries.content:
DETROIT — Abdul El-Sayed called Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of his Republican opponent in the Michigan Senate race a “distraction” on Sunday.

Stevens, a Michigan Democrat who El-Sayed defeated in the Senate primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers earlier in the day. Her decision to back Rogers drew criticism from other Democrats who said the focus should be on beating him, in a race that could help determine which party controls the Senate.

“This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government,” El-Sayed told reporters outside of Northend Church of God in Christ in Detroit. “I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about.”

El-Sayed, whose campaign has tried to steer the message back to Rogers, tried to address the needs of Michiganders rather than the drama created by Stevens.

“At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens,” he said when asked if Stevens had betrayed the Democratic Party. “I think about the, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I'm just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”

Stevens was originally slated to appear alongside El-Sayed and other high-profile Democrats at the event at the church on Sunday, before she demanded he apologize for his past criticism of Israel. She was eventually uninvited from the event.

Instead, she appeared with Rogers at church before releasing her endorsement.

El-Sayed, a progressive, was flanked by high-profile Democratic surrogates who traveled to the state to campaign, including Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland). Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who is running in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District against Republican candidate T.P. Nykoriak and other third-party candidates, also appeared.

Clyburn, a centrist Democrat with a lot of sway within the Democratic party, began his remarks to reporters by saying that El-Sayed’s campaign showed that the Democratic Party is the “party of a big tent.”

“Everything else is a distraction from what we're all about, and we know what we have in this young man for the future of this country,” Clyburn said, not directly mentioning the controversy or calling Stevens by name.

There’s skepticism among Democrats that Stevens’ endorsement will ultimately affect the race. But it did prompt immediate rebukes from national Democrats.

"I’m very disappointed," Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), who endorsed Stevens in the Senate Democratic primary, told The Washington Sun in a text. "Instead of working in a vacuum and making decisions hastily, under stress, she should have reached out and asked for help. So many people in our caucus would have been more than willing to talk her [through] this and offer sage advice. Instead, she burned everything that she worked hard to build, down in a time frame of 24 hours. And, at the end of the day, [it] buys her absolutely nothing."

He added: "Abdul is going to win. Abdul got this!”

Still, the endorsement was campaign fodder for Republicans, for everyone from Rogers to President Donald Trump.

As the press conference wrapped up, reporters continued to shout questions at El-Sayed including, “Does this change the outcome of the race?”

El-Sayed, looking frustrated with the questions about Stevens, responded: “None of this matters.”

He pointed down the block and said families nearby who are struggling to feed their children and pay medical bills matter more.

“The rest of this is just a distraction.”
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: Justice Department Urges Sanctions for Analysis Critical of Its Noncitizen Voting Claims
entries.summary: The DOJ said an immigrant rights group and its lawyers should face contempt charges after they published an analysis of the names.
entries.content:
By Nicholas Riccardi

The Justice Department on Sunday defended the accuracy of a list of what it says are more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens registered to vote in California and suggested that a federal judge consider whether an immigrant rights group and its lawyers should face contempt charges after they published an analysis of the names.

On Friday, U.S. District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg allowed the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, access to federal government data on 20,000 people the Trump administration alleges are noncitizen voters in California. Boasberg, based in Washington, D.C., ordered the plaintiffs not to disclose any names on the list and use the data only for their arguments about why they have legal standing to challenge the Trump administration's use of it.

On Saturday, attorneys for the immigrant rights group filed court papers revealing that their analysis found more than 40% of the people on the list do not appear in the state's voter file. It also identified 22 people on the list who were likely naturalized U.S. citizens while saying that thousands more U.S. citizens appeared to be on it, as well.

The Justice Department said in a filing Sunday that the analysis by the immigrant rights group had nothing to do with the group's legal standing and therefore violated Boasberg's order.

“The report’s political grandstanding about alleged inaccuracies that purportedly impact California voters generally, or comparisons between the government’s list and the full ‘California voter file,’ has no relevance to whether the particular plaintiffs in this case have standing,” it said.

The filing also suggested Boasberg refer the matter to the Justice Department for investigation for possible criminal contempt of court.

Alberto Lammers, a spokesman for the University of California, Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project, which filed the case and did the data analysis for the immigrant rights group, said in an emailed statement: “Plaintiffs’ counsel and their experts fully complied with the Court’s orders.”

In a separate case, the Justice Department on Sunday also appealed a decision from Friday night by U.S. District Court Judge Trina L. Thompson. The ruling by the San Francisco-based judge barred the department from demanding that election offices remove possible noncitizens from voter rolls, separate their ballots or threaten legal action. The Justice Department has noted that Thompson ruled before the federal government was able to file its initial arguments.

Thompson scheduled a Monday hearing on the appeal.

That case is one of many the Trump administration has lost in its battle over its lists of alleged noncitizen voters. A federal judge in California rejected its demand that election officials there be forced to separate ballots cast by those voters, writing that such last-minute orders could “wreak havoc” on the state's election. Two appellate judges agreed.

California election officials also contend the list is riddled with errors and say they have no way to do the painstaking work required by law to remove voters from the rolls in the days before the election. People attest to being U.S. citizens when they register to vote and risk felony prosecution if they cast a ballot when they are not eligible.

The administration has said its list was carefully compiled from the state's own voter registration data and compared to federal citizenship records. The Justice Department issued a series of subpoenas for election offices in California and warned election officials who knowingly let noncitizens vote that they could face criminal charges.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Nine People Aboard a Jet That Crashed in Florida Have Died
entries.summary: The private jet, flying from Texas to the Bahamas, nose-dived into the ground near a busy highway.
entries.content:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation's transportation secretary said.

Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a “horrific tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation, he said.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.

“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”

Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.

The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).

Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.

A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it crashed steeply into the ground.

Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet, according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.

But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.

“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.

“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”

Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.

Palm Beach County authorities are evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.

The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff’s officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

This story has been updated with further information on the location of the crash.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Plans to Deliver Closing Election Remarks at the Reflecting Pool
entries.summary: The president, who will speak on the eve of the midterms, has spent the past month traversing the country to host rallies ahead of Election Day.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will deliver remarks Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a White House official told The Washington Sun.

The president’s remarks are likely to serve as a closing message for his monthslong campaign rally blitz ahead of the midterms. In more than two dozen in-person rallies across the country, Trump has stumped for Republicans facing competitive statewide races, including for Senate nominees Ken Paxton in Texas and Mike Rogers in Michigan.

The president has often encouraged crowds at the rallies to vote as if he was on the ballot and has said Democratic victories would pose a threat to the policies he has been able to enact during the first two years of his second term.

During Trump’s second administration, the president has focused on renovating many D.C. landmarks, including the Reflecting Pool.

Trump has maintained that vandals cut the bottom of the pool, which his administration hired contractors to resurface with “American Flag Blue.” Shortly after completion in late June, chunks of the material could be seen partially detached in the water and algae blooms began to turn the pool bright green.

Trump told reporters in Iowa on Sunday he planned to deliver remarks at the Reflecting Pool “to show how beautiful it is.”

The Reflecting Pool has been the site of many historic speeches and events, particularly those associated with the civil rights movement. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial overlooking the Reflecting Pool in 1963, and President Barack Obama marked the 50th anniversary of King’s speech at the pool in 2013.
